You know that the husband must give up one-third of his share; accordingly he retains twice as much as that which is detracted from his share for the legacy. As he has three parts in hand, one of these falls to the legacy, and the remaining two parts he retains for himself. The two legacies together are imposed upon the son. It is therefore necessary to subtract from his share two-fifths and one-fourth of the same. He thus retains seven twentieths of his entire original share, dividing the whole of it into twenty equal parts. The mother retains as much as she contributes to the legacy; this is one (twelfth part), the entire amount of what she had received being two parts.

Take now a sum, one-fourth of which may be divided into thirds, or of one-sixth of which the moiety may be taken; this being again divisible by twenty. Such a capital is two hundred and forty. The mother receives one-sixth of this, namely, forty; twenty from this fall to the legacy, and she retains twenty for herself. The husband receives one-fourth, namely, sixty; from which twenty belong to the legacy, so that he retains forty. The remaining hundred and forty belong to the son; the legacy from this is two-fifths and one-fourth, or ninety-one; so that there remain forty-nine. The entire sum for the legacies is, therefore, one hundred and thirty-one, which must be divided among the two legatees. The one to whom two-fifths were bequeathed, receives eight-thirteenths of this; the one to whom one-fourth was devised, receives five-thirteenths.

If you wish distinctly to express the shares of the two legatees, you need only to multiply the parts of the heritage by thirteen, and to take them out of a capital of three thousand one hundred and twenty.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent\textbf{On another Species of Legacies.}\hfill\textnormal{\arterm{في نوع آخر من الوصايا}}

``A man dies, and leaves four sons and his wife; and bequeaths to a person as much as the share of one of the sons less the amount of the share of the widow.''

Divide the heritage into thirty-two parts. The widow receives one-eighth, namely, four; and each son seven. Consequently the legatee must receive three-sevenths of the share of a son. Add, therefore, to the heritage three-sevenths of the share of a son, that is to say, three parts, which is the amount of the legacy. This gives thirty-five, from which the legatee receives three and the remaining thirty-two are distributed among the heirs proportionably to their legal shares.

If he leaves two sons and a daughter, and bequeaths to some one as much as would be the share of a third son, if he had one; then you must consider, what would be the share of each son, in case he had three. Assume this to be seven, and for the entire heritage take a \no, one-fifth of which may be divided into sevenths, and one-seventh of which may be divided into fifths. Such a \no is thirty-five. Add to it two-sevenths of the same, namely, ten. This gives forty-five. Herefrom the legatee receives ten, each son fourteen, and the daughter seven.

If he leaves a mother, three sons, and a daughter, and bequeaths to some one as much as the share of one of his sons less the amount of the share of a second daughter, in case he had one; then you distribute the heritage into such a \no of parts as may be divided among the actual heirs, and also among the same, if a second daughter were added to them. Such a \no is three hundred and thirty-six. The share of the second daughter, if there were one, would be thirty-five, and that of a son eighty; their difference is forty-five, and this is the legacy. Add to it three hundred and thirty-six, the sum is three hundred and eighty-one, which is the \no of parts of the entire heritage.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent\textbf{On Completement.}\hfill\textnormal{\arterm{في الاستكمال}}

``A woman dies and leaves eight daughters, a mother, and her husband, and bequeaths to some person as much as must be added to the share of a daughter to make it equal to one-fifth of the capital and to another person as much as must be added to the share of the mother to make it equal to one-fourth of the capital.''

Computation: Determine the parts of the residue, which in the present instance are thirteen. Take the capital, and subtract from it one-fifth of the same, less one part, as the share of a daughter: this being the first legacy. Then subtract also one-fourth, less two parts, as the share of the mother: this being the second legacy. There remain eleven-twentieths of the capital, which, when increased by three parts, are equal to thirteen parts. Remove now from thirteen parts the three parts on account of the three parts (on the other side), and you retain eleven-twentieths of the capital, equal to ten parts. Complete the capital, by adding to the ten parts as much as nine-elevenths of the same; then you find the capital equal to eighteen parts and two-elevenths. Assume now each part to be eleven; then the whole capital is two hundred, each part is eleven; the first legacy will be twenty-nine, and the second twenty-eight.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent\textbf{Computation of Returns.}\hfill\textnormal{\arterm{في حساب المرتدات}}

\textit{On Marriage in Illness.}\hfill\textnormal{\arterm{في الزوج في المرض}}

``A man, in his last illness, marries a wife, paying (a marriage settlement of) one hundred \dirhems, besides which he has no property, her dowry being ten \dirhems. Then the wife dies, bequeathing one-third of her property. After this the husband dies.''

Computation: You take from the one hundred that which belongs entirely to her, on account of the dowry, namely, ten \dirhems; there remain ninety \dirhems, out of which she has bequeathed a legacy. Call the sum given to her (by her husband, exclusive of her dowry) \thn; subtracting it, there remain ninety \dirhems less \thn. Ten \dirhems and \thn are already in her hands; she has disposed of one third of her property, which is three \dirhems and one-third, and one-third of \thn; there remain six \dirhems and two-thirds plus two-thirds of \thn, the moiety of which, namely, three \dirhems and one-third plus one-third of \thn, returns as his portion to the husband. Thus the heirs of the husband obtain (as his share) ninety-three \dirhems and one-third, less two thirds of \thn; and this is twice as much as the sum given to the woman, which was \thn, since the woman had power to bequeath one-third of all which the husband left; and twice as much as the gift to her is two \things. Remove now the ninety-three and one-third, from two-thirds of \thn, and add these to the two \things. Then you have ninety-three \dirhems and one-third equal to two \things and two-thirds. One \thn is three-eighths of it, namely, as much as three-eighths of the ninety-three and one-third, that is, thirty-five \dirhems.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent\textbf{On Emancipation in Illness.}\hfill\textnormal{\arterm{في العتق في المرض}}

``Suppose that a man on his death-bed were to emancipate two slaves; the master himself leaving a son and a daughter. Then one of the two slaves dies, leaving a daughter and property to a greater amount than his price.'' You take two-thirds of his price, and what the other slave has to return (in order to complete his ransom). If the slave die before the master, then the son and the daughter of the latter partake of the heritage, in such proportion, that the son receives as much as the two daughters together. But if the slave die after the master, then you take two-thirds of his value and what is returned by the other slave, and distribute it between the son and the daughter (of the master), in such a manner, that the son receives twice as much as the daughter; and what then remains (from the heritage of the slave) is for the son alone, exclusive of the daughter; for the moiety of the heritage of the slave descends to the daughter of the slave, and the other moiety, according to the law of succession, to the son of the master, and there is nothing for the daughter (of the master).

It is the same, if a man on his death-bed emancipates a slave, besides whom he has no capital, and then the slave dies before his master.

If a man in his illness emancipates a slave, besides whom he possesses nothing, then that slave must ransom himself by two-thirds of his price. If the master has anticipated these two-thirds of his price and has spent them, then, upon the death of the master, the slave must pay two-thirds of what he retains.\footnote{The slave retains one-third of his price; and this he must redeem at two-thirds of its value; namely at $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{9}$ of his original price.} But if the master has anticipated from him his whole price and spent it, then there is no claim against the slave, since he has already paid his entire price.

``Suppose that a man on his death-bed emancipates a slave, whose price is three hundred \dirhems, not having any property besides; then the slave dies, leaving three hundred \dirhems and a daughter.'' The computation is this: Call the legacy to the slave \thn. He has to return the remainder of his price, after the deduction of the legacy, or three hundred less \thn. This ransom, of three hundred less \thn, belongs to the master. Now the slave dies, and leaves \thn and a daughter. She must receive the moiety of this, namely, one half of \thn; and the master receives as much. Therefore the heirs of the master receive three hundred less half a \thn, and this is twice as much as the legacy, which is \thn, namely, two \things. Reduce this by removing half a \thn from the three hundred, and adding it to the two \things. Then you have three hundred, equal to two \things and a half. One \thn is, therefore, as much as two-fifths of three hundred, namely, one hundred and twenty.

This is the legacy (to the slave,) and the ransom is one hundred and eighty.

``Some person on his sick-bed has emancipated a slave, whose price is three hundred \dirhems; the slave then dies, leaving four hundred \dirhems and ten \dirhems of debt, and two daughters, and bequeathing to a person one-third of his capital; the master has twenty \dirhems debts.'' The computation of this case is the following: Call the legacy to the slave \thn; his ransom is the remainder of his price, namely, three hundred less \thn. But the slave, when dying, left four hundred \dirhems; and out of this sum, his ransom, namely, three hundred less \thn, is paid to the master, so that one hundred \dirhems and \thn remain in the hands of the slave's heirs. Herefrom are (first) subtracted the debts, namely, ten \dirhems; there remain then ninety \dirhems and \thn. Of this he has bequeathed one-third, that is, thirty \dirhems and one-third of \thn; so that there remain for the heirs sixty \dirhems and two-thirds of \thn. Of this the two daughters receive two-thirds, namely, forty \dirhems and four-ninths of \thn, and the master as much. Therefore the heirs of the master altogether obtain three hundred and seventy less one-ninth of \thn; and this is twice as much as is given for the legacy, which is \thn. Reduce this, namely, subtract one-ninth from two; there remain one \thn and eight-ninths, equal to three hundred and seventy. One \thn is, therefore, nine-seventeenths of three hundred and seventy, that is, one hundred and ninety-six and two-seventeenths. The ransom is one hundred and three and fifteen-seventeenths.

\clearpage

\vspace{1cm}
\begin{center}
\rule{0.5\textwidth}{1pt}\\[0.5cm]
{\small\textit{End of the Translation of the Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa.}}
\end{center}

%% ========================================================================
%% APPENDIX A: NOTES ON THE ARABIC TEXT
%% ========================================================================
\section*{Notes on the Arabic Text}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Notes on the Arabic Text}

The following brief notes are intended to point out for further enquiry a few circumstances connected with the history of Algebra:

\begin{enumerate}

\item The initial words of the treatise, as cited by Haji Khalfa, are: \arterm{قال ابو عبدالله محمد بن موسى الخوارزمي} (``Abu Abdallah Mohammed ben Musa of Khowarezm said...'').

\item The term \aljabr (\term{الجبر}{al-jabr}) literally signifies ``\term{restoration}{الجبر}'' or ``completion,'' referring to the operation of transferring negative quantities to the other side of an equation as positive. The term \almuqabala (\term{المقابلة}{al-muqabala}) means ``\term{reduction}{المقابلة}'' or ``opposition,'' referring to the process of cancelling like quantities on both sides of an equation.

\item The Arabic word \shay (\term{شيء}{shay'}, literally ``thing'') is used throughout the text as the designation of the unknown quantity---what we should now call $x$. It corresponds exactly to the \textit{res} (``thing'') of the early Italian algebraists, and to the \textit{coss} of the Germans.

\item The word \mal (\term{مال}{m\=al}, literally ``property,'' ``wealth,'' ``possession'') is used to denote the \sq of the unknown. It is rendered by Rosen as ``\term{square}{مال}.''

\item The word \jidhr (\term{جذر}{jidhr}, literally ``root'') is used in the same sense as our ``root.'' The word \term{واجب}{w\=ajib} (literally ``obligatory'') is used for the ``absolute \no''---what we call the constant term.

\item The method of geometrical demonstration here employed by al-Khwarizmi is worthy of especial notice. It shows that, like the Greek mathematicians, he was not satisfied with merely giving rules, but endeavoured to establish their accuracy by demonstration. His proofs are founded upon the second proposition of Book II of Euclid's Elements, and upon the well-known property of the gnomon.

\item The formula for the circumference of a circle given in the text (Text p.~51, Transl. p.~72) is $c = \frac{62832}{20000}d$, which gives $\pi = 3.1416$. This value was known to the Hindu mathematician Aryabhata, and the circumstance furnishes a strong argument for the opinion that al-Khwarizmi derived part of his information from an Indian source.

\item The comparisons drawn between the Algebra of the Arabs and that of the early Italian writers might perhaps have been more numerous and more detailed; but the enquiry was here restricted by the want of some important works. Montucla, Cossali, Hutton, and the Basil edition of Cardanus' \textit{Ars magna}, were the only sources which the translator had the opportunity of consulting.

\item The solutions which the author has given of the remaining problems of this treatise, are, mathematically considered, for the most part incorrect. It is not that the problems, when once reduced into equations, are incorrectly worked out; but that in reducing them to equations, arbitrary assumptions are made, which are foreign or contradictory to the data first enounced, for the purpose, it should seem, of forcing the solutions to accord with the established rules of inheritance, as expounded by Arabian lawyers.

\item The object of the lawyers in their interpretations, and of the author in his solutions, seems to have been, to favour heirs and next of kin; by limiting the power of a testator, during illness, to bequeath property, or to emancipate slaves; and by requiring payment of heavy ransom for slaves whom a testator might, during illness, have directed to be emancipated.

\end{enumerate}

\clearpage

\section*{Appendix B: Arabic--English Glossary of Algebraic Terms}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix B: Arabic--English Glossary}

\begin{center}
{\Large\scshape\color{titlecolor} Complete Arabic--English Glossary}\\[0.3cm]
{\normalsize of Mathematical and Legal Terms in al-Khw\=arizm\=i's}\\[0.2cm]
{\large\textit{Kit\=ab al-Jabr wa-l-Muq\=abala}}\\[0.5cm]
\rule{0.5\textwidth}{1pt}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5cm}

\begin{arabicblock}
This glossary provides a comprehensive reference for the Arabic mathematical terminology employed throughout al-Khw\=arizm\=i's \textit{Kit\=ab al-Jabr wa-l-Muq\=abala}, with their English equivalents as established in Rosen's 1831 translation. The Arabic terms are given in their original grammatical form as they appear in the manuscript.
\end{arabicblock}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% SECTION 1: CORE ALGEBRAIC TERMS
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{I. Core Algebraic Terms}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{مال} & \textit{m\=al} (pl. \textit{amw\=al}) & \textbf{Square} of the unknown quantity; literally ``wealth,'' ``property,'' or ``possession.'' Denotes $x^2$. This is the central term of al-Khw\=arizm\=i's algebra: the square of the unknown \term{thing}{شيء}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{جذر} & \textit{jidhr} (pl. \textit{judh\=ur}) & \textbf{Root}; literally ``root,'' ``base,'' or ``origin.'' Denotes the unknown quantity $x$ itself, when referred to as a root to be extracted. In geometric contexts, also the side of a square. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{شيء} & \textit{shay'} (pl. \textit{ashy\=a'}) & \textbf{Thing}; the unknown quantity, corresponding to our $x$. The fundamental designation of the variable. Also rendered by Rosen as ``\term{root}{جذر}'' in many contexts. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{عدد} & \textit{'adad} (pl. \textit{a'd\=ad}) & \textbf{Number}; the constant or absolute term in an equation, not multiplied by any unknown. Simple, known quantities. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{واجب} & \textit{w\=ajib} & \textbf{Obligatory} term; used for the constant or absolute number that ``belongs'' to an equation. Sometimes used interchangeably with \term{number}{عدد}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{درهم} & \textit{dirham} (pl. \textit{dar\=ahim}) & \textbf{Dirhem}; the standard monetary unit, used as the concrete unit for numerical examples. Corresponds to the Greek drachma and the Roman denarius. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مضروب} & \textit{ma\d{r}\=ub} & \textbf{Product}; the result of multiplication. Literally ``the multiplied.'' \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{قسمة} & \textit{qismah} & \textbf{Division}; the operation of dividing one quantity by another. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{ناتج} & \textit{n\=atij} & \textbf{Result} or \textbf{quotient} of an operation. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{باق} & \textit{b\=aqin} & \textbf{Remainder}; what is left after subtraction or division. \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% SECTION 2: THE TWO FUNDAMENTAL OPERATIONS
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{II. The Two Fundamental Operations: \alJabr and \alMuqabala}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{الجبر} & \textit{al-jabr} & \textbf{Restoration} or \textbf{Completion}; the fundamental operation of transferring negative quantities from one side of an equation to the other as positive terms. Literally ``the setting of a broken bone,'' hence ``restoration to wholeness.'' This is the operation from which the entire science takes its name: \textit{Algebra}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{جبر} & \textit{jabr} & The verbal noun: to restore, to complete. When we ``complete'' a partial square to make it a whole square, we perform \aljabr. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{المقابلة} & \textit{al-muq\=abala} & \textbf{Reduction} or \textbf{Opposition}; the operation of cancelling like quantities on both sides of an equation. Literally ``the act of placing opposite'' or ``comparison.'' \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مقابلة} & \textit{muq\=abala} & The verbal noun: to reduce, to set opposite. When we subtract equal terms from both sides, we perform \almuqabala. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{رد} & \textit{radd} & \textbf{Reduction} by returning; another term for simplifying an equation. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{توحيد} & \textit{taw\h{e}id} & \textbf{Unification}; reducing multiple squares (or other terms) to a single square. \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% SECTION 3: THE SIX CANONICAL CASES
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{III. The Six Canonical Cases}

Al-Khw\=arizm\=i classifies all solvable equations into six fundamental types, which form the backbone of his method. These are traditionally grouped into three simple and three compound forms.

\vspace{0.3cm}

\textbf{The Three Simple Cases:}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{المساواة} & \textit{mus\=aw\=ah} & \textbf{Equality}; the condition of two quantities being equal. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{المسألة الأولى} & \textit{al-mas'ala al-\=ul\=a} & \textbf{First case}: \Squares equal to \Roots ($ax^2 = bx$) \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{المسألة الثانية} & \textit{al-mas'ala al-th\=aniya} & \textbf{Second case}: \Squares equal to \Numbers ($ax^2 = c$) \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{المسألة الثالثة} & \textit{al-mas'ala al-th\=alitha} & \textbf{Third case}: \Roots equal to \Numbers ($bx = c$) \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.3cm}

\textbf{The Three Compound Cases:}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{المسألة الرابعة} & \textit{al-mas'ala al-r\=abi'a} & \textbf{Fourth case}: \Roots and \Squares equal to \Numbers ($ax^2 + bx = c$) \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{المسألة الخامسة} & \textit{al-mas'ala al-kh\=amisa} & \textbf{Fifth case}: \Squares and \Numbers equal to \Roots ($ax^2 + c = bx$) \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{المسألة السادسة} & \textit{al-mas'ala al-s\=adisa} & \textbf{Sixth case}: \Roots and \Numbers equal to \Squares ($ax^2 = bx + c$) \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% SECTION 4: GEOMETRICAL TERMS
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{IV. Geometrical Terms}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{شكل} & \textit{shakl} (pl. \textit{ashk\=al}) & \textbf{Figure} or \textbf{form}; any geometric construction. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مربع} & \textit{murabba'} & \textbf{Quadrate} or \textbf{square}; a four-sided figure with equal sides and right angles. Distinct from \term{m\=al}{مال} (the algebraic square). \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{طول} & \textit{t\=ul} & \textbf{Length}; the longer dimension of a figure. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{عرض} & \textit{'ar\d{d}} & \textbf{Breadth} or \textbf{width}; the shorter dimension. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{قطر} & \textit{qa\d{t}r} (pl. \textit{qu\d{t}\=ur}) & \textbf{Diagonal} or \textbf{diameter}; a line connecting opposite corners of a quadrilateral, or passing through the centre of a circle. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{محيط} & \textit{mu\h{e}\=i\d{t}} & \textbf{Circumference} or \textbf{perimeter}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مساحة} & \textit{mis\=a\h{a}h} & \textbf{Area}; the measure of surface contained within a figure. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مثلث} & \textit{muthallath} & \textbf{Triangle}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{قائم الزاوية} & \textit{q\=a'im al-z\=awiya} & \textbf{Rectangular} (right-angled); literally ``erect of angle.'' \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{وتر} & \textit{watar} & \textbf{Hypotenuse} of a right-angled triangle. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{سهم} & \textit{sahm} & \textbf{Arrow} of a circular segment; the sagitta. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{وتر القوس} & \textit{watar al-qaws} & \textbf{Chord} of an arc. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{منحنى} & \textit{mun\h{ha}n\=a} & \textbf{Curve} or \textbf{arc}. \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% SECTION 5: ARITHMETICAL OPERATIONS
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{V. Arithmetical Operations}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{جمع} & \textit{jam'} & \textbf{Addition}; to collect quantities together. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{طرح} & \textit{tar\h{h}} & \textbf{Subtraction}; to remove one quantity from another. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{ضرب} & \textit{\d{d}arb} & \textbf{Multiplication}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{تكرير} & \textit{takr\=ir} & \textbf{Duplication}; doubling or repeated addition. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{تثليث} & \textit{tathl\=ith} & \textbf{Triplication}; trebling. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{نصف} & \textit{ni\d{s}f} & \textbf{Half}; the moiety of a quantity. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{ثلث} & \textit{thulth} & \textbf{Third}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{ربع} & \textit{rub'} & \textbf{Fourth} or \textbf{quarter}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{خمس} & \textit{khumus} & \textbf{Fifth}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{سدس} & \textit{sudus} & \textbf{Sixth}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{سبع} & \textit{sub'} & \textbf{Seventh}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{ثمن} & \textit{thumn} & \textbf{Eighth}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{تسع} & \textit{tus'} & \textbf{Ninth}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{عشر} & \textit{'ashr} & \textbf{Tenth}. \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% SECTION 6: COMMERCIAL AND LEGAL TERMS
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{VI. Commercial and Legal Terms}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{مكايلة} & \textit{mak\=ayala} & \textbf{Mensuration}; the art of measuring land and quantities. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مكايلة الأرض} & \textit{mak\=ayala al-ar\d{d}} & \textbf{Land-measurement} or \textbf{surveying}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{تجارة} & \textit{tij\=ara} & \textbf{Commerce} or \textbf{trade}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{ميرة} & \textit{m\=ira} & \textbf{Proportion} or \textbf{alloy}; used in problems of exchange and mixing. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مقايضة} & \textit{muq\=ayad.a} & \textbf{Exchange} or \textbf{barter}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{إجارة} & \textit{ij\=ara} & \textbf{Hire} or \textbf{rental}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{وصية} & \textit{was.iyya} & \textbf{Legacy} or \textbf{bequest}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{تركة} & \textit{tarika} & \textbf{Inheritance} or \textbf{estate} of the deceased. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{مواريث} & \textit{maw\=ar\=ith} & \textbf{Laws of inheritance}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فرائض} & \textit{far\=a'i\d{d}} & \textbf{Obligatory shares}; the fixed fractional shares prescribed by Islamic law for heirs. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{عصبة} & \textit{'a\d{s}aba} & \textbf{Residuaries}; heirs who take the remainder after the fixed shares have been distributed. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{رأس المال} & \textit{ra's al-m\=al} & \textbf{Capital} or \textbf{principal sum}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{ربح} & \textit{rib\h{h}} & \textbf{Profit} or \textbf{gain}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{دين} & \textit{dain} & \textbf{Debt} or \textbf{loan}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{دينار} & \textit{d\=in\=ar} & \textbf{Dinar}; the gold coin, counterpart to the silver \term{dirhem}{درهم}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فلس} & \textit{fals} & \textbf{Fals}; a copper coin of small value. \\

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% SECTION 7: VERBAL FORMS
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{VII. Common Verbal Constructions}

\begin{longtable}{@{}p{3.2cm}p{2.5cm}p{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic Term} & \textbf{Transliteration} & \textbf{Meaning and Usage} \\
\midrule
\endhead

\arterm{قل} & \textit{qul} & \textbf{Say} or \textbf{suppose}; the imperative opening most problems. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فإذا} & \textit{fa-idh\=a} & \textbf{Then if}; introducing the working of a problem. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فأصبح} & \textit{fa-a\d{s}ba\h{h}} & \textbf{Then it became}; the result of an operation. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فاجعل} & \textit{fa-ij'al} & \textbf{Then make} or \textbf{set}; used when introducing the unknown. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فاضرب} & \textit{fa-\d{d}rib} & \textbf{Then multiply}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فاجمع} & \textit{fa-ijma'} & \textbf{Then collect} or \textbf{add}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فاستخرج} & \textit{fa-istakhrij} & \textbf{Then extract}; as in extracting a root. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{فانظر} & \textit{fa-un\d{z}ur} & \textbf{Then observe} or \textbf{behold}. \\
\addlinespace

\arterm{إن شاء الله} & \textit{in sh\=a' All\=ah} & ``\textbf{God willing}''; a pious formula often found in Arabic mathematical manuscripts.

\bottomrule
\end{longtable}

\vspace{0.5cm}

%% ========================================================================
%% NOTES ON THE GLOSSARY
%% ========================================================================
\subsection*{Notes on the Glossary}

\begin{enumerate}

\item \textbf{On the term \alJabr:} The word derives from the root \arterm{ج ب ر} (\textit{j-b-r}), meaning ``to set a broken bone,'' ``to restore,'' or ``to make whole.'' In the algebraic context, it refers specifically to the restoration of completeness in an equation by transferring subtracted (negative) quantities to the other side as added (positive) quantities. The science of \textit{algebra} takes its name from this fundamental operation.

\item \textbf{On the term \alMuqabala:} Derived from the root \arterm{ق ب ل} (\textit{q-b-l}), meaning ``to place opposite'' or ``to compare,'' this operation consists in setting like terms against each other on opposite sides of an equation and cancelling them. Together, \aljabr and \almuqabala reduce any equation to one of the six canonical forms.

\item \textbf{On \textit{m\=al} and \textit{jidhr}:} The distinction between these terms is fundamental. \term{M\=al}{مال} (square) is the \textit{quantity} $x^2$; \term{jidhr}{جذر} (root) is either the \textit{quantity} $x$ or the \textit{operation} of extracting a square root. \term{Shay'}{شيء} (thing) is the unknown itself before it has been determined. The modern reader may think of: \textit{shay'} = $x$, \textit{m\=al} = $x^2$, \textit{jidhr} = $\sqrt{x^2} = x$.

\item \textbf{On \textit{w\=ajib}:} This term, meaning ``obligatory'' or ``necessary,'' is used for the absolute (constant) term because it ``must'' be present as an obligation in the equation---it cannot be eliminated by the operations of \aljabr or \almuqabala.

\item \textbf{The threefold terminology for the unknown:} Arabic algebraists employed a subtle three-level terminology: \term{shay'}{شيء} for the unknown quantity in its algebraic sense, \term{jidhr}{جذر} when referring to it as the root of a square (especially in extraction), and \term{ \no}{عدد} when it has been determined to a numerical value.

\item \textbf{Dirhem and Dinar:} The \term{dirhem}{درهم} was the standard silver coin of the Islamic world; the \term{d\=in\=ar}{دينار} was the gold coin, worth approximately 10--20 dirhems depending on time and place. The \term{fals}{فلس} was a copper coin of fractional value.

\item \textbf{On the six cases:} Al-Khw\=arizm\=i's classification is exhaustive for equations involving only positive coefficients and positive solutions. The possibility of negative roots was not admitted; equations leading to such results were pronounced ``impossible'' (\arterm{مستحيل}). The restriction to positive coefficients is what necessitates six cases rather than the modern unified quadratic formula.

\item \textbf{Geometrical vs.\ algebraic terminology:} The reader should note that al-Khw\=arizm\=i uses \term{murabba'}{مربع} for the geometrical figure (quadrate) and \term{m\=al}{مال} for the algebraic square of the unknown. This distinction, carefully maintained in the Arabic, is sometimes blurred in Rosen's translation.

\end{enumerate}

\vspace{1cm}
\begin{center}
\rule{0.5\textwidth}{1pt}\\[0.5cm]
{\small\textit{End of Glossary}}
\end{center}

%% APPENDIX C: HOW TO READ THE BILINGUAL EDITION

\section*{Appendix C: Guide to this Bilingual Edition}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix C: Guide to this Bilingual Edition}

\begin{arabicblock}
This enhanced bilingual edition employs a system of inline Arabic annotations designed to preserve the full text of Rosen's classic 1831 English translation while restoring the original Arabic terminology of al-Khw\=arizm\=i's \textit{Kit\=ab al-Jabr wa-l-Muq\=abala}.
\end{arabicblock}

\vspace{0.3cm}

\textbf{How the annotations work:}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Primary terms:} The first occurrence of each technical term in a section appears as \term{English}{Arabic}, e.g., \term{square}{مال}, \term{root}{جذر}, \term{thing}{شيء}, \term{number}{عدد}, \term{restoration}{الجبر}, \term{reduction}{المقابلة}, \term{dirhem}{درهم}.

\item \textbf{Shorthand references:} Subsequent occurrences in the same section use abbreviated macros: \sq, \ro, \thn, \no, \di, \alJabr, \alMuqabala.

\item \textbf{Arabic block quotations:} Passages set in small type within quotation environments provide explanatory notes on the Arabic terminology.

\item \textbf{Case headers:} Each of the six canonical cases carries its Arabic title in the header line.

\item \textbf{Footnotes:} Rosen's original mathematical footnotes are preserved in their entirety.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.3cm}

\textbf{The six Arabic terms restored throughout:}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Arabic} & \textbf{Transliteration} \\
\midrule
\term{square}{مال} & \arterm{مال} & \textit{m\=al} \\
\term{root}{جذر} & \arterm{جذر} & \textit{jidhr} \\
\term{thing}{شيء} & \arterm{شيء} & \textit{shay'} \\
\term{number}{عدد} & \arterm{عدد} & \textit{'adad} \\
\term{restoration}{الجبر} & \arterm{الجبر} & \textit{al-jabr} \\
\term{reduction}{المقابلة} & \arterm{المقابلة} & \textit{al-muq\=abala} \\
\term{dirhem}{درهم} & \arterm{درهم} & \textit{dirham} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.3cm}

\textbf{Editions Consulted and Reference Works:}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Original edition:} Frederic Rosen, \textit{The Algebra of Mohammed ben Musa}, London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1831. Arabic text with English translation.

\item \textbf{Manuscript source:} Bodleian Library, Oxford, MS Hunt. 214 (Cod. CXVIII), folios 1--67, transcribed A.H. 743 (A.D. 1342).

\item \textbf{Related works:} Haji Khalfa, \textit{Kashf al-\d{Z}un\=un}; Ibn Khallikan, \textit{Wafay\=at al-A'y\=an}; Casiri, \textit{Bibliotheca Arabico-Hispana Escurialensis}; Colebrooke, \textit{Algebra, with Arithmetic and Mensuration from the Sanscrit of Brahmegupta and Bhascara} (1817).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{paracol}{2}

\section*{Einleitung}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Introduction / Einleitung}

\textit{Da\ss{} die Mathematik bei den Arabern aus indischen und griechischen Quellen zusammengeflossen ist und vielfach durch Perser, Syrer und Juden in den Strom des geistigen Lebens eingef"uhrt wurde, ist eine Tatsache, die sich ebenso deutlich aus dem Inhalt der arabischen Schriften und der literarischen "Uberlieferung ergibt, wie sie der geschichtlichen Lagerung der islamischen Gesamtkultur entspricht.}

\switchcolumn

\section*{Introduction}

\textit{That mathematics among the Arabs flowed together from Indian and Greek sources, and was frequently introduced into the stream of intellectual life by Persians, Syrians, and Jews, is a fact that emerges as clearly from the content of Arabic writings and literary tradition as it corresponds to the historical stratification of Islamic culture as a whole.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Schwierigeren Fragen stehen wir aber alsbald gegen"uber, wenn wir diese allgemein anerkannte Abh"angigkeit auf bestimmte Quellen zur"uckf"uhren wollen, wenn wir die auf lange Strecken versch"utteten Rinnsale aufzudecken versuchen, in denen die Zufuhr des fremden Stoffes sich vollzog, und wenn wir eine Entscheidung dar"uber treffen sollen, ob ein bestimmtes Wissen seine Form schon auf dem Weg zur Sammelstelle erhalten hat oder erst dem arabischen Einflu\ss{} seine Gestaltung verdankt.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{But we immediately face more difficult questions when we wish to trace this generally acknowledged dependence back to specific sources, when we try to uncover the streams that have been covered over for long stretches through which the supply of foreign material occurred, and when we must decide whether a particular body of knowledge received its form already on the way to its destination or owes its shaping to Arabic influence.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Die Schwierigkeiten wachsen, wenn sich Urteile "uber solche Dinge nicht auf die Quellen erster Hand, sondern auf "Ubersetzungen und Bearbeitungen st"utzen, die den Charakter des Originalwerks verwischt haben und vielfach schon von pers"onlicher Stellungnahme bestimmt sind.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The difficulties increase when judgments about such matters rest not on first-hand sources but on translations and reworkings that have obscured the character of the original work and are frequently already determined by personal bias.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{F"ur alle Untersuchungen, die die Form der Darstellung betreffen, also f"ur die ganze Geschichte der Terminologie, werden wir daher immer wieder auf die Originalquellen zur"uckgehen m"ussen, um zu neuen oder gesicherteren Ergebnissen zu gelangen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{For all investigations concerning the form of presentation, that is, for the entire history of terminology, we shall therefore always have to return to the original sources in order to arrive at new or more secure results.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Eine erneute Untersuchung der "altesten arabischen Algebra schien besonders aussichtsvoll, nachdem sich bei einem fl"uchtigen Vergleich herausgestellt hatte, da\ss{} die von Fr.\ Rosen 1831 dem Text der Algebra des Muhammad b.\ M"us"a al-Hw"arazm"i beigef"ugte "Ubersetzung nicht den Wortlaut wiedergibt, sondern sich ziemlich gro\ss{}e Freiheiten gestattet.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{A renewed investigation of the earliest Arabic algebra seemed especially promising after a cursory comparison had revealed that the translation appended by Fr.\ Rosen in 1831 to the text of the Algebra of Muhammad b.\ M"us"a al-Khw"arizm"i does not reproduce the wording but allows itself rather great liberties.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Sie schien auch darum erw"unscht, weil "uber die Grundlagen der arabischen Algebra so viele entgegengesetzte und sich ausschlie\ss{}ende Ansichten ge"au\ss{}ert worden sind, da\ss{} von einer Ersch"opfung des Gegenstandes noch immer nicht gesprochen werden kann.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{It also seemed desirable because so many contradictory and mutually exclusive views have been expressed about the foundations of Arabic algebra that an exhaustive treatment of the subject cannot yet be spoken of.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Im weiteren Verlauf der Arbeit stellte sich dann die Notwendigkeit heraus, auch andere Texte und "Ubersetzungen in den Bereich der Untersuchung zu ziehen, und so ist schlie\ss{}lich eine Reihe von mehr oder minder zusammenh"angenden Einzelbeitr"agen zur Geschichte der "alteren arabischen Mathematik entstanden.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{In the further course of the work, the necessity arose to bring other texts and translations into the scope of the investigation, and thus finally a series of more or less connected individual contributions to the history of older Arabic mathematics has emerged.}

\switchcolumn*

\textbf{Anmerkung zur Namensumschreibung.} \textit{Man kann eine ganze Musterkarte von Umschreibungen dieses Namens zusammenstellen; so schreibt Colebrooke (1817) Khuw"arezmi, Rosen (1831) of Khio war ezm, Woepcke (1863) Alkh"arizmi, Marre (1865) Al Kh"ar e z m, Rodet (1878) Al-Kh"arizmi, Hankel (1874) al-Hov"arezmi, Cantor (1880) Alchwarizmi, van Vloten (1895) Al-Khowarezmi, Suter (1900) el-Chow"aresml oder Chw"aresml, Bj"ornbo (1905) Alkwarizmi, Wiedemann (1906) al Ch"arizmi, Bosmans (1906) El-Chow"arizmi, Karpinski (1910) Al-Khowarizmi, Smith (1911) Al-Khow"arazmi, Enestr"om Alkhwarizmi und Alkwarismi.}

\switchcolumn

\textbf{Note on the Rendering of the Name.} \textit{A complete pattern card of renderings of this name can be assembled; thus Colebrooke (1817) writes Khuw"arezmi, Rosen (1831) of Khio war ezm, Woepcke (1863) Alkh"arizmi, Marre (1865) Al Kh"ar e z m, Rodet (1878) Al-Kh"arizmi, Hankel (1874) al-Hov"arezmi, Cantor (1880) Alchwarizmi, van Vloten (1895) Al-Khowarezmi, Suter (1900) el-Chow"aresml or Chw"aresml, Bj"ornbo (1905) Alkwarizmi, Wiedemann (1906) al Ch"arizmi, Bosmans (1906) El-Chow"arizmi, Karpinski (1910) Al-Khowarizmi, Smith (1911) Al-Khow"arazmi, Enestr"om Alkhwarizmi and Alkwarismi.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Sowenig wir das Wort Averroismus durch Ibnrusdismus ersetzen k"onnen, so wenig ist die moderne Umschreibung Alhw"arazmi geeignet, die Erinnerung an die Algorithmiker lebendig zu erhalten.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Just as little as we can replace the word Averroism with Ibn-Rushd-ism, so little is the modern transcription Alhw"arazmi suited to keeping alive the memory of the algorists.}

\end{paracol}

\clearpage

% ============================================================
% SECTION I: Der Titel der Algebra
% ============================================================
\begin{paracol}{2}

\section{Der Titel der Algebra des Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a}

\textit{Erw"ahnte Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a nicht selbst in der Einleitung zu seiner \enquote{Algebra} die Gegenst"ande, von denen er zu handeln beabsichtigt, so k"onnte man versucht sein, das uns erhaltene Werk als willk"urliche Zusammenf"ugung von zwei oder drei urspr"unglich getrennten Schriften anzusehen.}

\switchcolumn

\section{The Title of the Algebra of Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a}

\textit{Had Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a not himself mentioned in the introduction to his \enquote{Algebra} the subjects he intended to treat, one might be tempted to regard the work preserved to us as an arbitrary compilation of two or three originally separate writings.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Sein Inhalt entspricht aber durchaus dem, was der Verfasser als seine Absicht bezeichnet:}

\begin{quote}
\arblock{ان هذا كتاب الاجابة والمقابلة وقد حددته الى ما يسهل من الحساب وما يحتاج اليه الناس في مواريثهم ووصاياهم ومقاسمتهم ومعاملتهم وكل ما يتداولونه بينهم من المكايلة والمساحة وغير ذلك}

\enquote{ein kurzgefa\ss{}tes Buch zu schreiben von dem Rechenverfahren der Erg"anzung und Ausgleichung (\textit{his\=ab al-gabr wa-l-muq\=abala}) mit Beschr"ankung auf das Anmutige und Hochgesch"atzte des Rechenverfahrens f"ur das, was die Leute fortw"ahrend notwendig brauchen bei ihren Erbschaften und ihren Verm"achtnissen und bei ihren Teilungen und ihren Proze\ss{}bescheiden und ihren Handelsgesch"aften und bei allem, womit sie sich gegenseitig befassen von der Ausmessung der L"andereien und der Herstellung der Kan"ale und der Geometrie und anderm dergleichen nach seinen Gesichtspunkten und Arten.}
\end{quote}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Its content, however, fully corresponds to what the author states as his intention:}

\begin{quote}
\arblock{ان هذا كتاب الاجابة والمقابلة وقد حددته الى ما يسهل من الحساب وما يحتاج اليه الناس في مواريثهم ووصاياهم ومقاسمتهم ومعاملتهم وكل ما يتداولونه بينهم من المكايلة والمساحة وغير ذلك}

\enquote{to write a concise book on the calculation procedure of restoration and balancing (\textit{his\=ab al-gabr wa-l-muq\=abala}), restricted to the elegant and esteemed aspects of calculation for what people perpetually need in their inheritances and their bequests and in their divisions and their legal verdicts and their commercial transactions, and in everything they engage in together concerning the measurement of lands and the construction of canals and geometry and other such things, according to its aspects and categories.}
\end{quote}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Der Verfasser gibt selbst nirgends eine Andeutung, woher er seinen Stoff hat, und wieweit ihm pers"onlich ein Verdienst an der Pr"agung zukommt. Halten wir uns gegenw"artig, da\ss{} er sich als Astronom anerkannterma\ss{}en auf indische Wissenschaft st"utzte und auch ein Buch "uber das indische Rechnen verfa\ss{}te, so ist die Richtung angegeben, in der man zun"achst zu suchen hat.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The author himself gives no indication anywhere of whence he obtained his material, nor to what extent he himself may claim credit for its formulation. Bearing in mind that he as an astronomer admittedly relied upon Indian science and also wrote a book on Indian calculation, the direction in which one must first search is indicated.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Man hat immer wieder dem Erstaunen Ausdruck gegeben, da\ss{} Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a seinem Werk einen Titel gegeben habe, den er nicht erkl"art, und da\ss{} er daf"ur zwei Operationen ausgew"ahlt habe, die in dem \enquote{eigentlich theoretischen Teile} seines Buches gar nicht vorkommen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{People have repeatedly expressed astonishment that Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a gave his work a title that he did not explain, and that he chose for it two operations that do not occur at all in the \enquote{properly theoretical part} of his book.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Ich glaube, man hat sich das Verst"andnis dieser Tatsachen ganz unn"otig erschwert, indem man das Buch nicht historisch mit den \enquote{Augen des Verfassers} (Cantor a.\ a.\ O.\ S.\ 728), sondern ohne R"ucksicht auf den Gesamtinhalt nur nach den wenigen theoretischen Kapiteln am Anfang beurteilte, die den Geschichtschreiber der Mathematik besonders interessieren.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{I believe that the understanding of these facts has been made quite unnecessarily difficult by judging the book not historically with the \enquote{eyes of the author} (Cantor \textit{op.\ cit.}, p.\ 728), but without regard to the total content, only according to the few theoretical chapters at the beginning that especially interest the historian of mathematics.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Schon H.\ Hankel hat mit dieser Verschiebung des Tatbestandes den Anfang gemacht, indem er zwar den Inhalt des ersten Teils der Algebra ganz zutreffend kennzeichnet, die geometrischen Kapitel aber davon losl"ost und von dem Rest des Werkes bemerkt, da\ss{} die dort behandelten Aufgaben "uber Erbteilungen von keinem wissenschaftlichen Interesse seien, wenn sie auch f"ur Mohammedaner praktisch von gr"o\ss{}tem Werte waren.\footnote{H.\ Hankel, \textit{Zur Geschichte der Mathematik in Alterthum und Mittelalter}, Leipzig 1874, S.\ 260.}}

\switchcolumn

\textit{H.\ Hankel already began this shifting of the facts, in that he indeed quite accurately characterized the content of the first part of the Algebra, but detached the geometrical chapters from it and remarked of the remainder of the work that the problems on inheritance treated there were of no scientific interest, even if they were of great practical value for Muslims.\footnote{H.\ Hankel, \textit{Zur Geschichte der Mathematik in Alterthum und Mittelalter}, Leipzig 1874, p.\ 260.}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Auf dieser Stufe der Untersuchung gen"ugt es, die Tatsache festzuhalten, da\ss{} Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a eine \enquote{Algebra} in unserem Sinne nicht schreiben wollte, noch geschrieben hat. Sein Buch will weiter nichts sein als eine auf zahlreiche ausgef"uhrte Musterbeispiele gest"utzte Einf"uhrung in das angewandte Rechnen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{At this stage of the investigation, it suffices to establish the fact that Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a neither wanted to write nor wrote an \enquote{Algebra} in our sense. His book wants to be nothing more than an introduction to applied calculation, supported by numerous worked-out model examples.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Wenn wir G"unther glauben sollen, w"u\ss{}te man erst \enquote{sp"ateren Berichten zufolge}, da\ss{} eine Gleichung f"ur \enquote{eingerichtet} galt, wenn auf beiden Seiten ausschlie\ss{}lich positive Glieder standen, w"ahrend das Wort \enquote{Gegen"uberstellung} dem Weglassen gleicher Gr"o\ss{}en links und rechts entsprach.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{If we are to believe G"unther, one knew only \enquote{according to later reports} that an equation counted as \enquote{arranged} when exclusively positive terms stood on both sides, while the word \enquote{opposition} corresponded to the removal of equal quantities from left and right.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Auch Cantor (I\textsuperscript{3}, S.\ 719) und Hankel (S.\ 260, Note**) berufen sich auf die Erkl"arungen sp"aterer arabischer Schriftsteller, und wer will, kann bei Rosen (S.\ 180\,ff.) oder Nesselmann (\textit{Die Algebra der Griechen}, S.\ 40\,ff.) Text und "Ubersetzung von Originalstellen nachlesen, in denen eine Erkl"arung der Ausdr"ucke \textit{al-gabr} und \textit{al-muq\=abala} gegeben wird.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Cantor (I\textsuperscript{3}, p.\ 719) and Hankel (p.\ 260, note**) also rely on the explanations of later Arabic writers, and whoever wishes can read in Rosen (p.\ 180\,ff.) or Nesselmann (\textit{Die Algebra der Griechen}, p.\ 40\,ff.) the text and translation of original passages in which an explanation of the expressions \textit{al-gabr} and \textit{al-muq\=abala} is given.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Kein Zweifel kann dar"uber bestehen, da\ss{} die verschiedenen "Ubersetzungen der beiden Termini eine klare Vorstellung von ihrem mathematischen Sinn nicht zu geben verm"ogen. \textit{Restauratio et oppositio} ist ein ebenso unklares Begriffspaar wie \textit{restoring and comparing} (Colebrooke) oder \textit{completion and reduction} (Rosen), \textit{Wiederherstellung und Gegen"uberstellung} (Cantor) oder \textit{Erg"anzung und Ausgleichung}, wie ich oben "ubersetzt habe.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{No doubt can exist that the various translations of the two terms are unable to give a clear idea of their mathematical sense. \textit{Restauratio et oppositio} is no clearer a pair of concepts than \textit{restoring and comparing} (Colebrooke) or \textit{completion and reduction} (Rosen), \textit{Wiederherstellung und Gegen"uberstellung} (Cantor), or \textit{Erg"anzung und Ausgleichung} [restoration and balancing], as I have translated above.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Gestehen wir aber dem Autor zu, da\ss{} wir ihn ganz gelesen haben m"ussen, ehe wir ihn kritisieren, so bekommen wir ein wesentlich anderes Bild. Wir begegnen den beiden Ausdr"ucken zuerst wieder da, wo der Verfasser ausf"uhrt, da\ss{} bei dem \textit{his\=ab al-gabr wa-l-muq\=abala} drei Arten von Zahlen vorkommen, die als \textit{gud"ur} d.\ i.\ Wurzeln, \textit{amw\=al} d.\ i.\ Verm"ogen, und \textit{radad mufrad} d.\ i.\ alleinstehende Zahl bezeichnet werden.\footnote{Ich gebe die Termini auch in Umschrift, weil die Leser, die sich f"ur Geschichte der Mathematik interessieren, mit der arabischen Schrift und Sprache nur ausnahmsweise Bescheid wissen.}}

\switchcolumn

\textit{But if we grant the author that we must have read him completely before criticizing him, we obtain a substantially different picture. We encounter the two expressions first where the author explains that in the \textit{his\=ab al-gabr wa-l-muq\=abala} three kinds of numbers occur, designated as \textit{gud"ur} that is, roots, \textit{amw\=al} that is, possessions [wealth/capital], and \textit{radad mufrad} that is, isolated number.\footnote{I also give the terms in transliteration, because readers interested in the history of mathematics are only rarely familiar with Arabic script and language.}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Hieraus ist noch nichts zu entnehmen. Aber schon S.\ 15, am Schlu\ss{} des theoretischen Teils, der die sechs Normalformen der Gleichungen behandelt, wird dem Leser gesagt, da\ss{} jede andere Gleichung durch das Verfahren der Erg"anzung und Ausgleichung auf eine der sechs Normalformen gebracht werden kann.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Nothing can yet be gathered from this. But already on p.\ 15, at the end of the theoretical part that treats the six normal forms of equations, the reader is told that every other equation can be brought to one of the six normal forms through the procedure of restoration and balancing.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Im ersten Beispiel, das in unserer Schreibweise zum Ansatz $x^{2} = 40x - 4x^{2}$ f"uhrt, kommt nur \enquote{Erg"anzung} vor. Nachdem der Ansatz abgeleitet ist, wird das Ergebnis ausdr"ucklich zusammengefa\ss{}t: \enquote{Es ist also ein Verm"ogen gleich vierzig Etwas weniger vier Verm"ogen} und fortgefahren: \enquote{Erg"anze es nun durch die vier Verm"ogen, und f"uge sie dem einen Verm"ogen hinzu, so werden vierzig Etwas gleich f"unf Verm"ogen; dann ist das einzelne Verm"ogen gleich acht Wurzeln} usw.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{In the first example, which in our notation leads to the equation $x^{2} = 40x - 4x^{2}$, only \enquote{restoration} [\textit{al-gabr}] occurs. After the equation is derived, the result is explicitly summarized: \enquote{So a quantity is equal to forty things less four quantities,} and it continues: \enquote{Restore it now by the four quantities and add them to the one quantity, so forty things become equal to five quantities; then a single quantity equals eight roots,} etc.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Man wird hiernach gewi\ss{} nicht mehr behaupten k"onnen, da\ss{} Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a diese Ausdr"ucke nirgends erkl"art hat, wie schon bei Rosen S.\ 177 zu lesen ist, zumal die verschiedenen Definitionen aus sp"aterer Zeit auch nur darauf hinauskommen, die \enquote{Erg"anzung} durch \enquote{Hinzuf"ugung} und die \enquote{Ausgleichung} durch \enquote{Wegnahme gleicher Gr"o\ss{}en} zu ersetzen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{After this, one will certainly no longer be able to claim that Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a has explained these expressions nowhere, as can already be read in Rosen, p.\ 177, especially since the various definitions from later times also amount merely to replacing \enquote{restoration} with \enquote{addition} and \enquote{balancing} with \enquote{removal of equal quantities.}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Kein Araber wird den Ausdruck \enquote{Erg"anzungs- und Ausgleichungsrechnung} mi\ss{}verstanden haben, wenn er sich in das Buch eingelesen hatte und im Text den Imperativen \enquote{erg"anze} oder \enquote{gleiche aus} mit den Anweisungen zur Ausf"uhrung der Rechnung begegnete.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{No Arab would have misunderstood the expression \enquote{restoration-and-balancing calculation} if he had read into the book and encountered in the text the imperatives \enquote{restore} or \enquote{balance} together with the instructions for carrying out the calculation.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Die Frage, ob Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a die beiden Ausdr"ucke \textit{al-gabr} und \textit{al-muq\=abala} als erster angewandt und in die Praxis der Gleichungen eingef"uhrt hat, oder ob er damit schon einer festen Tradition und alten "Ubung folgte, wird nur im Zusammenhang mit der Pr"ufung der gesamten Terminologie und literarischen Form seines Werkes der L"osung n"aher gebracht werden k"onnen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The question whether Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a was the first to apply the two expressions \textit{al-gabr} and \textit{al-muq\=abala} and introduced them into the practice of equations, or whether he was already following a fixed tradition and old usage, can only be brought closer to solution in connection with the examination of the entire terminology and literary form of his work.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Der allgemeinste aus einer Textaufgabe zu gewinnende Ansatz f"uhrt zur Gleichsetzung zweier Ausdr"ucke, die durch Addition, Subtraktion, Multiplikation und Division bekannter und unbekannter Gr"o\ss{}en entstehen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The most general equation obtainable from a word problem leads to the equating of two expressions that arise through addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of known and unknown quantities.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Zu diesen beiden wichtigsten Operationen kommt dann noch \textit{al-radd}, die \enquote{Zur"uckf"uhrung} des Koeffizienten der Unbekannten auf 1, wenn er gr"o\ss{}er als 1 ist, und \textit{al-ikm\=al}, die \enquote{Vervollst"andigung}, wenn der Koeffizient ein echter Bruch ist. Dies ist der Tatbestand, den wir in der "altesten Algebra vorfinden.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{To these two most important operations are added \textit{al-radd}, the \enquote{reduction} of the coefficient of the unknown to 1 when it is greater than 1, and \textit{al-ikm\=al}, the \enquote{completion}, when the coefficient is a proper fraction. This is the state of affairs that we find in the earliest algebra.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{F"ur die weitere Geschichte des Wortes \enquote{Algebra} ist es von Interesse, da\ss{} es schon bei den I\hw{}\=an a\s-s{}af\=a', also um das Jahr 1000, ohne den Begriff \textit{muq\=abala} zur Bildung des Wortes \enquote{Algebraiker} gebraucht wird.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{For the further history of the word \enquote{Algebra} it is of interest that already among the I\hw{}\=an a\s-s{}af\=a' [Brethren of Purity], thus around the year 1000, the concept \textit{muq\=abala} was dispensed with in forming the word \enquote{algebraist.}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Endlich ist einer Erweiterung des Begriffs \textit{al-gabr} zu gedenken, die sich bereits im Rechenbuch des al-Kar\v{a}g\=i{} (gest.\ um 1030) vorfindet. Sie besteht darin, da\ss{} al-Kar\v{a}g\=i{} auch die Wegschaffung von Br"uchen, also das, was Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a als \textit{ikm\=al} bezeichnet, unter den Begriff \textit{gabr} subsumiert.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Finally, an extension of the concept \textit{al-gabr} is to be noted, which is already found in the arithmetic book of al-Kar\v{a}g\=i{} (d.\ ca.\ 1030). It consists in the fact that al-Kar\v{a}g\=i{} also subsumes the removal of fractions---that which Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a designates as \textit{ikm\=al}---under the concept \textit{gabr}.}

\end{paracol}

\clearpage

% ============================================================
% SECTION II: Liber augmenti et diminutionis
% ============================================================
\begin{paracol}{2}

\section{Das Liber augmenti et diminutionis und das kit\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q}

\textit{Es w"are nicht notwendig gewesen, so lange bei dem Titel der Algebra zu verweilen, wenn nicht von der Deutung der Termini das Verst"andnis der ganzen Entwicklung der Mathematik abhinge, und wenn nicht schon in den Titeln der mathematischen Schriften ein St"uck Geschichte enthalten w"are.}

\switchcolumn

\section{The \textit{Liber augmenti et diminutionis} and the \textit{Kit\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q}}

\textit{It would not have been necessary to dwell so long on the title of the Algebra if the understanding of the entire development of mathematics did not depend on the interpretation of these terms, and if a piece of history were not already contained in the titles of mathematical writings.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Ich denke hierbei nat"urlich auch an das von Libri 1838 im ersten Band seiner \textit{Histoire des Sciences Math\'ematiques en Italie} S.\ 304\,ff.\ ver"offentlichte \textit{Liber augmenti et diminutionis} und die Vermutungen, die "uber den Inhalt einer Schrift des Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a ge"au\ss{}ert worden sind, von der uns nur der Titel \textit{kit\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q} "uberliefert ist.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{I naturally think here also of the \textit{Liber augmenti et diminutionis}, published by Libri in 1838 in the first volume of his \textit{Histoire des Sciences Math\'ematiques en Italie}, pp.\ 304\,ff., and of the conjectures that have been expressed about the content of a writing of Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a, of which only the title \textit{Kit\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q} [Book of Aggregation and Dispersion] has been transmitted to us.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Hier liegen Schwierigkeiten, um deren Kl"arung und Beseitigung man seit Jahrzehnten bem"uht ist. Woepcke scheint der erste gewesen zu sein, der den arabischen Titel \textit{al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q} dem "uber \textit{augmenti et diminutionis} gleichsetzte (J.\ As., 6.\ S., Bd.\ I, 1863, S.\ 514).}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Here lie difficulties whose clarification and removal have been sought for decades. Woepcke seems to have been the first to equate the Arabic title \textit{al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q} with \textit{augmenti et diminutionis} (\textit{Journal Asiatique}, 6th ser., vol.\ I, 1863, p.\ 514).}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Es ist jedoch h"ochst zweifelhaft, ob man diese beiden Titel miteinander identifizieren darf, denn \enquote{Vermehrung} hei\ss{}t arabisch nicht \textit{\u0357{}am'}, und \enquote{Verminderung} hei\ss{}t nicht \textit{tafr\={i}q}. \textit{Liber augmenti et diminutionis} w"urde arabisch \textit{kit\=ab al-ziy\=ada wa-l-nuqs\=an} hei\ss{}en, w"ahrend ein \textit{kit\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q} etwa mit \textit{liber de aggregatione et dispersione} zu "ubersetzen w"are.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{It is, however, highly doubtful whether one may identify these two titles with each other, for \enquote{increase} is in Arabic not \textit{\u0357{}am'}, and \enquote{decrease} is not \textit{tafr\={i}q}. \textit{Liber augmenti et diminutionis} would in Arabic be called \textit{Kit\=ab al-ziy\=ada wa-l-nuqs\=an}, while a \textit{Kit\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-tafr\={i}q} would be translated approximately as \textit{Liber de aggregatione et dispersione}.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Das Verfahren der Vermehrung und Verminderung ist bekannter unter dem Namen der Regel der \enquote{zwei Fehler} (\textit{reg.\ elchatayn} = \ar{الخطأين}) oder des doppelten falschen Ansatzes, auch als \enquote{Regel der zwei Wagschalen}.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The method of increase and decrease is better known under the name of the rule of \enquote{two errors} (\textit{reg.\ elchatayn} = \ar{الخطأين}) or the double false position, also as the \enquote{rule of the two scales}.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Die stets wiederkehrenden Wendungen \textit{errasti per \ldots{} addita} oder \textit{cum \ldots{} additis}, \textit{errasti per \ldots{} diminuta} oder \textit{cum \ldots{} diminutis} entsprechen arabischem \ar{زدت} bzw.\ \ar{نقصت} und k"onnen nicht durch \textit{ziy\=adat} oder \textit{nuqs\=an} wiedergegeben werden.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The constantly recurring expressions \textit{errasti per \ldots{} addita} or \textit{cum \ldots{} additis}, \textit{errasti per \ldots{} diminuta} or \textit{cum \ldots{} diminutis} correspond to the Arabic \ar{زدت} [you have added too much] and \ar{نقصت} [you have fallen short], and cannot be rendered by \textit{ziy\=adat} or \textit{nuqs\=an}.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Einen letzten Beweis f"ur die Verschiedenheit der beiden Titel kann man daraus ableiten, da\ss{} der Mathematiker Ab"u K\=amil \u015e\=uc\=a' b.\ Aslam sowohl ein Buch "uber die zwei Fehler, als eines "uber \textit{\u0357{}am'} und \textit{tafr\={i}q} verfa\ss{}te.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{A final proof of the distinctness of the two titles can be derived from the fact that the mathematician Ab"u K\=amil \u015e\=uc\=a' b.\ Aslam wrote both a book on the two errors and one on \textit{\u0357{}am'} and \textit{tafr\={i}q}.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Solange nicht aus dem Inhalt noch zu entdeckender Werke oder mit anderen zwingenden Gr"unden nachgewiesen ist, da\ss{} die beiden Titel gleichbedeutend sind, wird man das Gegenteil als richtig oder wahrscheinlich annehmen m"ussen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{As long as it is not proved from the content of works yet to be discovered or by other compelling reasons that the two titles are synonymous, one must assume the opposite as correct or probable.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Was kann aber nun in einem Werke "uber \textit{\u0357{}am'} und \textit{tafr\={i}q} enthalten gewesen sein? Da\ss{} es sich um irgendwelche Kapitel der Rechenkunst oder der Algebra handelt, ergibt sich zweifellos daraus, da\ss{} der Titel stets in Verbindung mit Schriften arithmetischen Inhalts erw"ahnt wird.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{But what might have been contained in a work on \textit{\u0357{}am'} and \textit{tafr\={i}q}? That it concerned some chapters of arithmetic or algebra follows doubtless from the fact that the title is always mentioned in connection with writings of arithmetic content.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Nun ist die n"achste Bedeutung von \textit{\u0357{}am'} die der \enquote{Vereinigung} oder \enquote{Summation}. In diesem Sinne wird \textit{\u0357{}ama'a} nicht weniger als viermal in dem obenerw"ahnten ersten Beispiel angewandt.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Now the nearest meaning of \textit{\u0357{}am'} is that of \enquote{union} or \enquote{summation}. In this sense \textit{\u0357{}ama'a} [he united] is used no fewer than four times in the above-mentioned first example.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Die Verbindung von \textit{\u0357{}am'} und \textit{tafr\={i}q} wird also eher den Gegensatz von Sammlung --- Zerstreuung oder von Vereinigung --- Trennung ausdr"ucken. Einen solchen Gegensatz finde ich auf dem Gebiet der Algebra nur in dem Kapitel von der Klammerrechnung.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The combination of \textit{\u0357{}am'} and \textit{tafr\={i}q} will thus more likely express the opposition of collection---dispersion or union---separation. I find such an opposition in the domain of algebra only in the chapter on parenthetical computation [bracket expansion].}

\end{paracol}

\clearpage

% ============================================================
% SECTION III: Die Regula Sermonis
% ============================================================
\begin{paracol}{2}

\section{Die Regula Sermonis}

\textit{Ich schlie\ss{}e an diese Er"orterungen noch eine Bemerkung "uber das in dem \textit{Liber augmenti et diminutionis} gelehrte Umkehrungsverfahren, das durch Cantor (I\textsuperscript{3}, S.\ 732) \enquote{unter dem sonderbaren Namen der Wortrechnung, \textit{regula sermonis}} in die Geschichte der Mathematik eingef"uhrt worden ist.}

\switchcolumn

\section{The \textit{Regula Sermonis}}

\textit{I append to these discussions one more remark about the reversal procedure taught in the \textit{Liber augmenti et diminutionis}, which was introduced into the history of mathematics by Cantor (I\textsuperscript{3}, p.\ 732) \enquote{under the strange name of word-calculation, \textit{regula sermonis}}.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Die Textstelle, auf die es ankommt, lautet (Libri S.\ 312): \enquote{\textit{Quaedam vero harum quaestionum investigantur secundum regulam quae vocatur infusa. Et ipsa est regula Job filii Salomonis divisoris\ldots{}}}}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The passage in question reads (Libri, p.\ 312): \enquote{\textit{Indeed certain of these questions are investigated according to the rule which is called infusa. And it is the rule of Job son of Solomon the divisor\ldots{}}}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Zun"achst ist klar, da\ss{} man das sinnlose \textit{infusa} durch \textit{inversa} zu ersetzen hat.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{First of all, it is clear that the meaningless \textit{infusa} must be replaced by \textit{inversa}.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Von h"ochstem Interesse ist weiter, da\ss{} das Verfahren auch die Regel des Erbteilers oder Testamentsvollstreckers Aiyy"ub b.\ Sulaim\=an genannt wird --- denn so ist das Wort \textit{divisor} nach einer Randnote der Handschrift zweifellos zu "ubersetzen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Of the highest interest, further, is the fact that the procedure is also called the rule of the heir-divider or testament-executor Aiyy"ub b.\ Sulaim\=an --- for thus the word \textit{divisor} is doubtless to be translated, according to a marginal note of the manuscript.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Wir erblicken darin eine Best"atigung der Vermutung, da\ss{} die Rechenkunst und die Kunst der Gleichungsaufl"osung nicht nur bei den Astronomen, sondern ganz besonders auch bei den Notaren und Rechtsgelehrten eine Pflegest"atte gefunden hat.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{We see in this a confirmation of the conjecture that the art of calculation and the art of equation-solving found a home not only among astronomers, but especially among notaries and legal scholars.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Wenn aber nun Cantor a.\ a.\ O.\ behauptet, da\ss{} dieses Verfahren bei den Arabern den sonderbaren Namen der Wortrechnung gef"uhrt habe, so zeigt ein Blick in den lateinischen Text und die R"uck"ubersetzung ins Arabische, da\ss{} diese Behauptung auf einem Mi\ss{}verst"andnis beruht.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{But if Cantor \textit{op.\ cit.} claims that this procedure bore among the Arabs the strange name of word-calculation, a glance at the Latin text and the retranslation into Arabic shows that this claim rests on a misunderstanding.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Es hei\ss{}t im Text nicht \textit{regula sermonis}, sondern \textit{regula sermonis eius}, und das ist weiter nichts als die w"ortliche Wiedergabe des arabischen \textit{qiy\=asu qaulih\={i}}, eines Ausdruckes, der nichts anderes besagt als \enquote{die Regel, die er angibt}.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The text does not say \textit{regula sermonis} but \textit{regula sermonis eius} [the rule of his speech], and that is nothing other than the literal rendering of the Arabic \textit{qiy\=asu qaulih\={i}}, an expression that means nothing other than \enquote{the rule that he gives.}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Die \enquote{Wortrechnung} wird also k"unftig aus der Liste der mathematischen Termini verschwinden m"ussen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The \enquote{word-calculation} must therefore disappear from the list of mathematical terms in the future.}

\end{paracol}

\clearpage


% ============================================================
% SECTION IV: Inhaltsuebersicht
% ============================================================
\begin{paracol}{2}

\section{Inhalts"ubersicht der Algebra Muhammad b.\ M"us\=as und Beurteilung ihrer Quellen}

\textit{Wir kehren zur Algebra des Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a zur"uck und verschaffen uns durch Zusammenstellung der Kapitel"uberschriften eine erste "Ubersicht des Inhalts. Es ist bekannt, da\ss{} der Text des Buches auf der einzigen Oxforder Handschrift CMXCVIII Hunt.\ 214 ruht, die im Jahre 743 d.\ H., also um 1342 vollendet wurde (Rosen, S.\ XIII).}

\switchcolumn

\section{Overview of the Contents of the Algebra of Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a and Assessment of Its Sources}

\textit{We return to the Algebra of Muhammad b.\ M"us\=a and obtain a first overview of the content by assembling the chapter headings. It is known that the text of the book rests on the unique Oxford manuscript CMXCVIII Hunt.\ 214, completed in the year 743 AH, that is, around 1342 (Rosen, p.\ XIII).}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Da\ss{} die von Libri im ersten Band seiner \textit{Geschichte} S.\ 253\,ff.\ ver"offentlichte "Ubersetzung des Gerhard von Cremona nur die ersten 50 Seiten des Originals, also nur die Algebra im engeren Sinne ohne die Geometrie und Erbteilungsrechnung umfa\ss{}t, war z.\ B.\ bis vor kurzem nirgends in geschichtlichen Werken vermerkt.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The fact that the translation of Gerard of Cremona published by Libri in the first volume of his \textit{Histoire}, pp.\ 253\,ff., covers only the first 50 pages of the original---thus only the Algebra in the narrower sense, without the geometry and inheritance calculation---was, for example, nowhere noted in historical works until recently.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Es ist klar, da\ss{} durch Unterdr"uckung der Einleitung, die ausdr"ucklich auch auf den geometrischen und erbrechtlichen Teil des Werkes hinwies, der Anschein erweckt wird, als sei das "ubersetzte Bruchst"uck das ganze Buch.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{It is clear that by suppressing the introduction, which explicitly referred also to the geometrical and inheritance-law parts of the work, the appearance is created that the translated fragment is the whole book.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Folgen wir der Kapiteleinteilung des arabischen Textes, so ergibt sich folgender Aufbau des Ganzen:}

\switchcolumn

\textit{If we follow the chapter division of the Arabic text, the following structure of the whole emerges:}

\switchcolumn*

\textbf{(Einleitung, S.\ 1, 2.)} \textit{Anrufung Gottes, Preis des Propheten, Schilderung der m"uhevollen Arbeit der Gelehrten, Bericht "uber die Veranlassung zur Abfassung und "uber den Zweck des Buches. [fehlt bei Libri]}

\switchcolumn

\textbf{(Introduction, pp.\ 1, 2.)} \textit{Invocation of God, praise of the Prophet, description of the laborious work of scholars, report on the occasion of composition and on the purpose of the book. [missing in Libri]}

\switchcolumn*

\textbf{[Erster Hauptteil --- ohne "Uberschrift; S.\ 3 bis 50.]} \textit{Aufbau des Zahlensystems; Definition der in dem Rechenverfahren der Erg"anzung und Ausgleichung auftretenden Arten (dur"ub) von Zahlen; Aufz"ahlung der drei einfachen F"alle von Gleichungen; sodann Beispiele.}

\switchcolumn

\textbf{[First Main Part --- without heading; pp.\ 3 to 50.]} \textit{Structure of the number system; definition of the kinds (dur"ub) of numbers occurring in the calculation procedure of restoration and balancing; enumeration of the three simple cases of equations; then examples.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Eine Schlu\ss{}bemerkung leitet "uber zu den geometrischen Beweisen der Aufl"osungen: \enquote{Und ich habe f"ur jedes Kapitel von ihnen eine Zeichnung gezeichnet, durch die auf den Grund der Halbierung hingewiesen wird.}}

\switchcolumn

\textit{A concluding remark leads over to the geometrical proofs of the solutions: \enquote{And I have drawn for each chapter of them a figure, through which the basis of halving is indicated.}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Das Kapitel von der Multiplikation (\ar{باب الضرب} \textit{b\=ab al-darb}; S.\ 15 bis 19 oben). Das Kapitel von der Addition (Aggregation) und Subtraktion (\ar{باب الجمع والنقصان} \textit{b\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-nuqs\=an}; S.\ 19, 20). Die Teilung (\ar{القسمة} \textit{al-qisma}; S.\ 20, 21).}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The chapter on multiplication (\ar{باب الضرب} \textit{b\=ab al-darb}; pp.\ 15 to 19 above). The chapter on addition (aggregation) and subtraction (\ar{باب الجمع والنقصان} \textit{b\=ab al-\u0357{}am' wa-l-nuqs\=an}; pp.\ 19, 20). Division (\ar{القسمة} \textit{al-qisma}; pp.\ 20, 21).}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Das Kapitel der sechs Fragen (S.\ 25 bis 29). Das Kapitel der vermischten Fragen (33 mehr oder minder ausf"uhrlich behandelte Beispiele; S.\ 30 bis 48 oben).}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The chapter of the six questions (pp.\ 25 to 29). The chapter of mixed questions (33 more or less extensively treated examples; pp.\ 30 to 48 above).}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Das Kapitel der kaufm"annischen Gesch"afte (\ar{باب المعاملات} \textit{b\=ab al-mu\=amal\=at}; drei Beispiele.\ S.\ 48 bis 50).}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The chapter of commercial transactions (\ar{باب المعاملات} \textit{b\=ab al-mu\=amal\=at}; three examples.\ pp.\ 48 to 50).}

\switchcolumn*

\textbf{[Zweiter Hauptteil --- ohne besondere Hervorhebung:]} \textit{Kapitel der Messung (S.\ 50 bis 64). Das Kapitel ist eine lose Aneinanderreihung von geometrischen Definitionen, Eigenschaften von Figuren und Formeln mit Hervorhebung durch Stichworte.}

\switchcolumn

\textbf{[Second Main Part --- without special emphasis:]} \textit{Chapter of mensuration (pp.\ 50 to 64). The chapter is a loose sequence of geometrical definitions, properties of figures, and formulas with emphasis through keywords.}

\switchcolumn*

\textbf{[Dritter Hauptteil --- mit Hervorhebung der "Uberschrift:]} \textit{Das Buch der Testamente (S.\ 65--122). Ein Kapitel davon "uber das Kapital und die Schuld (S.\ 65 bis 67; drei durchgerechnete Beispiele). Ein anderes Kapitel von den Testamenten (S.\ 67, 68; zwei erl"auterte Beispiele).}

\switchcolumn

\textbf{[Third Main Part --- with emphasis of the heading:]} \textit{The book of testaments (pp.\ 65--122). A chapter thereof on capital and debt (pp.\ 65 to 67; three worked-through examples). Another chapter on testaments (pp.\ 67, 68; two explained examples).}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Das Kapitel von der Vervollst"andigung (\ar{باب التكميلة} \textit{b\=ab al-takm\={i}la}, S.\ 93 bis 98; sieben Beispiele).}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The chapter of completion (\ar{باب التكميلة} \textit{b\=ab al-takm\={i}la}, pp.\ 93 to 98; seven examples).}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Das Rechenverfahren bei Schicksalswechsel (\ar{حساب الدور} \textit{his\=ab al-daur}, \textit{computation of returns}).\footnote{Die "Ubersetzung von Rosen ist falsch. Das Wort \textit{daur} bezeichnet die wechselseitige Vertauschung (A gegen B, B gegen A), in unserm Falle Vertauschung von Erblasser und Erben, wenn der Erbe vorher stirbt.}}

\switchcolumn

\textit{The calculation procedure for reversal of fortune (\ar{حساب الدور} \textit{his\=ab al-daur}, \textit{computation of returns}).\footnote{Rosen's translation is incorrect. The word \textit{daur} designates the mutual exchange (A for B, B for A), in our case the exchange of testator and heir when the heir dies first.}}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Schon diese Inhalts"ubersicht kann zum Nachdenken "uber die Gr"unde anregen, die den Verfasser veranla\ss{}t haben, drei nach unserer Auffassung ganz heterogene Gegenst"ande unter dem Sammeltitel \textit{kit\=ab al-gabr wa-l-muq\=abala} zu vereinigen.}

\switchcolumn

\textit{Even this overview of contents can prompt reflection on the reasons that induced the author to unite three subjects that are, in our view, quite heterogeneous under the collective title \textit{Kit\=ab al-gabr wa-l-muq\=abala}.}

\end{paracol}

\clearpage

% ============================================================
% SECTION V: Zur Geschichte der arabischen Zahlbezeichnungen
% ============================================================
\begin{paracol}{2}

\section{Zur Geschichte der arabischen Zahlbezeichnungen}

\textit{Es kann nicht oft und nachdr"ucklich genug gesagt werden, da\ss{} die Araber, die die persischen und r"omischen Provinzen "uberfluteten, weder Rechtswissenschaft noch Staatsverwaltung fertig mitbrachten, sondern gezwungen waren, die Verwaltungsmethoden und Rechtsformen der eroberten L"ander im wesentlichen unver"andert zu "ubernehmen.}

\switchcolumn

\section{On the History of Arabic Numeral Designations}

\textit{It cannot be said often or emphatically enough that the Arabs who flooded the Persian and Roman provinces brought neither jurisprudence nor state administration ready-made with them, but were compelled to take over the administrative methods and legal forms of the conquered lands essentially unchanged.}

\switchcolumn*

\textit{Das w"are aber gewi\ss{} unm"oglich gewesen, wenn der geistige Abstand zwischen dem Eroberervolk und den zeitgen"ossischen Persern, Griechen und "Agyptern so gro\ss{} gewesen w"are, wie man bis in die neueste Zeit anzunehmen pflegte.}

\switchcolumn
