%% ===== APPENDIX: THE DUST BOARD METHOD =====
\section*{Appendix: The Dust Board (\textit{Takht}) Calculation Method}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix: The Dust Board (\textit{Takht}) Calculation Method}

\begin{enhancednote}
The \textit{takht} (Persian ``board'' or ``tablet'') or \textit{ab\=ak} was the primary computing surface used with Hindu-Arabic numerals for centuries. A wooden board was covered with fine sand or dust, and calculations were performed by drawing numerals with a stylus. The ``figures of the dust'' (\textit{arq\=am al-gub\=ar} / \ar{أرقام الغبار}) gave their name to the Western Arabic numeral system.
\end{enhancednote}

\textbf{How the Dust Board Worked:}

The calculation process on the \textit{takht} proceeded as follows:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Setting up}: The board was sprinkled with fine dark sand or dust. A smooth, dark surface made the drawn numerals visible.

  \item \textbf{Writing}: Numerals were inscribed with a pointed stylus (\textit{mud\=i}). Each digit of a multi-digit number was written in its proper place-value column.

  \item \textbf{Calculation}: Operations proceeded by writing intermediate results, erasing previous values, and shifting numbers place-by-place. This \textit{galley} or \textit{scratch} method explains why algorithmic arithmetic was once called ``ciphering''---the numerals were literally scratched in dust.

  \item \textbf{Erasures}: After each intermediate step, the used numerals were smoothed away, leaving only the current result. This explains the scarcity of early worked examples in manuscripts---the medium was ephemeral.

  \item \textbf{Final result}: When the computation was complete, the result could be either read aloud, copied to parchment, or left on the board.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{arabicpassage}
\textbf{From a 12th-century Arabic treatise on the dust method:}

\vspace{0.5em}
\ar{والحساب على التربة يحتاج إلى أن يكون الرجل سريعًا في الكشط والإثبات، وإذا أراد أن يضرب عددًا في عدد فليضع أحدهما على التربة ثم يضرب فيه العدد الآخر منزلًا منزلة.}

\vspace{0.5em}
\textit{Translation}: ``And calculation on the dust board requires that a man be swift in erasing and fixing; and if he wishes to multiply a number by a number, let him place one of them on the board, then multiply by it the other number, place by place."
\end{arabicpassage}

\textbf{Multiplication on the \textit{Takht} --- An Example:}

To multiply $437 \times 28$ on the dust board:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|c|l|}
\hline
\textbf{Step} & \textbf{Action} \\
\hline
1 & Write 437 on the board, right-aligned \\
2 & Write 8 (units of multiplier) below 437 \\
3 & Multiply 8$\times$7 = 56; erase 7, write 6, carry 5 \\
4 & Multiply 8$\times$3 = 24 + 5 = 29; erase 3, write 9, carry 2 \\
5 & Multiply 8$\times$4 = 32 + 2 = 34; erase 4, write 34 \\
6 & Result of $8 \times 437$: \quad 3\,4\,9\,6 \\
7 & Erase the 8; write 2 (tens of multiplier) shifted one place left \\
8 & Multiply 2$\times$437 = 874; add to previous result by columns \\
9 & Final result: \quad 1\,2\,2\,3\,6 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

This step-by-step procedure, working from right to left and erasing at each stage, is the origin of the modern long multiplication algorithm. The term ``algorithm'' itself derives from the corruption of al-Khw\=arizm\=i's name in the Latin incipit \textit{Dixit algoritmi}.

\vspace{0.5em}
\begin{center}
\textit{Algorithmus} $\leftarrow$ \textit{Algorismus} $\leftarrow$ \textit{al-Khw\=arizm\=i}
\end{center}

\newpage

%% ===== APPENDIX: THE EASTERN AND WESTERN FORMS COMPARED =====
\section*{Appendix: Eastern and Western Arabic Numeral Forms}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Appendix: Eastern and Western Arabic Numeral Forms}

\begin{enhancednote}
The divergence between Eastern (Hind\=i, used in Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Persia) and Western (gub\=ar, used in Spain, Morocco, Tunisia) Arabic numeral forms is one of the key facts in the transmission to Europe. The European forms descended not from the Eastern numerals used in Baghdad, but from the Western forms used in al-Andalus and the Maghrib.
\end{enhancednote}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\rowcolor{tableheader}
\textbf{Digit} & \textbf{Eastern Arabic} & \textbf{Western Arabic} & \textbf{Modern European} \\
\hline
0 & \ar{٠} & $\circ$ / $\cdot$ & 0 \\
\hline
1 & \ar{١} & \ar{١} / $1$ & 1 \\
\hline
2 & \ar{٢} & \ar{٢} / $\mathfrak{2}$ & 2 \\
\hline
3 & \ar{٣} & \ar{٣} / $\digamma$ & 3 \\
\hline
4 & \ar{٤} & \ar{٤} / $h$ & 4 \\
\hline
5 & \ar{٥} & \ar{٥} / $b$ & 5 \\
\hline
6 & \ar{٦} & \ar{٦} / $6$ & 6 \\
\hline
7 & \ar{٧} & \ar{٧} / $V$ & 7 \\
\hline
8 & \ar{٨} & \ar{٨} / $\infty$ & 8 \\
\hline
9 & \ar{٩} & \ar{٩} / $g$ & 9 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{1em}
\textbf{Key Distinguishing Features:}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=3pt]
  \item \textbf{The Eastern 5} \ar{٥} has a distinctive ``top-knot'' or loop at the top, resembling a small zero above a stroke. The Western 5 evolved into our modern form.

  \item \textbf{The Eastern 4} \ar{٤} resembles our modern 4 but with a closed top. The Western 4 passed through an ``h''-like stage before becoming our open-topped 4.

  \item \textbf{The Eastern 6} \ar{٦} is written from the bottom up. The Western 6 retained a form closer to our modern numeral.

  \item \textbf{The Eastern 7} \ar{٧} has a distinct top stroke. The Western 7 lost this stroke to become our plain 7.

  \item \textbf{The zero}: Both systems used a dot \textperiodcentered\ or small circle. The circle form prevailed in the West and became standard.
\end{itemize}

\newpage

%% ===== CONCLUSION =====
\section*{Conclusion}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{Conclusion}

In conclusion, we may say that the history of the Hindu-Arabic numerals is a long and complex one, stretching over many centuries and involving many different civilizations. From their earliest beginnings in India, through their development by the Arabs, to their final adoption in Europe, these numerals have had a remarkable career. They are one of the most important inventions in the history of civilization, and their influence on science, commerce, and daily life can hardly be overestimated.

The study of their history reveals the deep connections that have always existed between the peoples of the East and the West, and shows how knowledge has been transmitted from one civilization to another along the great trade routes that have linked the world since ancient times. It is a story that deserves to be known by all who use these symbols, which have become so familiar that we are apt to forget how much labor and ingenuity went into their creation.

\begin{enhancednote}
\textbf{Summary of the Transmission Pathway:}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
\textbf{Stage} & \textbf{Time} & \textbf{Key Evidence} \\
\hline
Brahmi numerals (no zero) & c.~250 B.C. & Asoka inscriptions \\
N\=an\=a Gh\=at forms & c.~150 B.C. & Cave inscriptions \\
Gupta period development & 4--6 c.~A.D. & Coins, inscriptions \\
Zero appears & c.~500--876 A.D. & Bh\=askara, Gwalior \\
\hline
Transmission to Arabs & 8--9 c.~A.D. & al-Khw\=arizm\=i, al-Fihrist \\
Eastern (Hind\=i) forms & 9--12 c. & Baghdad school \\
Western (gub\=ar) forms & 10--13 c. & Spain, Maghrib \\
\hline
Fibonacci's \textit{Liber Abaci} & 1202 A.D. & Latin manuscripts \\
European diffusion & 13--16 c. & Commercial arithmetic \\
General adoption & 17--18 c. & Printed textbooks \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\end{enhancednote}
